certainty_reasoning: The page gives an existing acquaintance ('A great friend of mine, a Paris boy called le petit Georges'), an arranged meeting Wilde has undertaken to keep ('I have promised to run over and see him'), and four clauses of physical praise. That is the same shape as rolla--wilde, which the corpus already classes attraction-expressed - a man written to or promised in advance, described, and looked forward to, with nothing recorded of what happened - and it is classed the same way here for consistency as well as on its merits. Against the README bar, a reader who does not hold the coding hypothesis reads an older man promising to travel to see a beautiful young man and dwelling on his face; the desire is legible without the hypothesis, though the reading is this project's and no scholarly source was consulted. romantic-nonsexual was weighed: 'a great friend of mine' and the promise do imply contact from Georges's side, which is more mutuality than the rest of this tier offers. It was rejected because every expression of feeling on the page is Wilde's, because 'friend' is not documented courtship, and because the class displays as 'Romantic'. documented-sexual is unavailable - no first-person statement of sexual relations appears. Recorded exactly and without gloss, because it bears on how the connection should be read: Wilde says Georges 'is visiting Nice on speculative business', and the paragraph continues, on the following printed page, with a remark about combining romance with business; that continuation was not read in the source and is carried below as a pointer. Whether Georges was selling sex is not stated on the page read, and no such finding is entered here. Standing caveat for this tier: the record is one-sided by nature. These men left no papers; everything known is what Wilde wrote to a friend. An unrecorded outcome is not evidence of no outcome - here Wilde states an intention to go to Nice, and no letter read says whether he and Georges met. SECOND PAGE ADDED 2026-08-05: printed 1108, read at the page, puts the same boy in Paris three weeks earlier - 'One beautiful boy of bad character - of the name of Georges … so like Antinous'. The editors' index ties the two pages to one person. This does not change the certainty class; it doubles the evidence for it and shows the acquaintance predated the Nice meeting Wilde had 'promised' to keep.
date_label: The intended meeting at Nice, announced in a letter postmarked 3 January 1899 from Napoule, for a trip 'tomorrow'. The friendship itself predates the letter - Wilde calls him a great friend and places him as a Paris boy - but no earlier date was verified in the source.
summary: From Napoule at the start of January 1899, Wilde told Reginald Turner that Harold Mellor was arriving that day and that the two of them were going to Nice the next day, where a great friend of his, a Paris boy he called 'le petit Georges', was then staying and whom he had promised to see. The letter gives four clauses of physical description and says Georges was at Nice on speculative business. Nothing read records whether the meeting took place.

sources.quote: Kalisaya, the American Bar near the Crédit Lyonnais, is now the literary resort of myself and my friends: and we all gather there at five o'clock - Moréas, and La Jeunesse, and all the young poets. One beautiful boy of bad character - of the name of Georges - goes there too, but he is so like Antinous, and so smart, that he is allowed to talk to poets.
sources.context: Wilde in Paris, December 1898, three weeks before the Nice letter. THE EDITORS INDEX THIS AS THE SAME BOY: their entry reads 'Georges (boy), 1097, 1108, 1117' - confirmed on the rendered index page - and printed 1117 is the 'le petit Georges' letter that this connection already rests on. INDEX SLIP WORTH RECORDING: the 1097 in that string is wrong. Printed 1097 carries only the letter to MONSIEUR Georges, the proprietor of L'Écu, whom Wilde thanks for a week's lodging and whose wife and parents he sends compliments to; he has his own index entry at the same page. A future sweep chasing 'Georges' should not merge them. Antinous was the boy the emperor Hadrian loved and deified after his death, and in Wilde's vocabulary the comparison is never neutral.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That Wilde knew him in Paris before Nice, and how he described him to a correspondent other than Turner.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1154; printed folio 1108 confirmed on the rendered page image. The editors' index entry confirmed on the rendered page image of PDF 1292. Both read 2026-08-05.

sources.quote: My friend, my new friend, Harold Mellor comes here today to stay at the hotel, and tomorrow we go to Nice, for the day. A great friend of mine, a Paris boy called le petit Georges, is now at Nice, and I have promised to run over and see him. He is like a very handsome Roman boy, dark, and bronze-like, with splendidly chiselled nose and mouth, and the tents of midnight are folded in his eyes; moons hide in their curtains. He is visiting Nice on speculative business.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Turner, [Postmark 3 January 1899], Hôtel des Bains, Napoule - the second paragraph of the letter, following the weather. 'le petit Georges' is italicised on the page. The paragraph continues past the last sentence quoted here onto printed 1118.
sources.supports: The whole of the verified record: an existing friendship, a promised meeting at Nice, Wilde's description of him, and the statement that he was at Nice on speculative business; no outcome recorded
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1163, printed folio 1117 confirmed at the foot of the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: A great friend of mine, a Paris boy called le petit Georges, is now at Nice, and I have promised to run over and see him. He is like a very handsome Roman boy, dark, and bronze-like, with splendidly chiselled nose and mouth, and the tents of midnight are folded in his eyes; moons hide in their curtains. He is visiting Nice on speculative business. It is beautiful, and encouraging, to find people who can combine romance with business – blend them indeed, and make them one.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Turner, postmark 3 January 1899, Hotel des Bains, Napoule. The sentence begun on p. 1117 completes on p. 1118.
sources.supports: How Wilde glosses Georges's 'speculative business' at Nice - the sentence completes on the following page and bears directly on how the connection should be read
